analysis.one_liner: Bans lawmakers and federal workers from trading stocks on nonpublic government information.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2007, referred to five House committees, and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the SEC and the futures regulator to write rules banning anyone from trading stocks or commodities while holding secret information about pending legislation learned through Congress or federal employment. It would bar House personnel from leaking such information for trading purposes, require members of Congress to report their own stock trades within 90 days, and force political-intelligence firms—companies that sell Washington information to investors—to register and disclose their contacts the same way lobbyists must. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and the general public. Trading on knowledge only insiders possess lets a favored few profit at the expense of everyone else in the market; the bill would close that gap for the most privileged insiders in Washington. It would also give the public a running record of lawmakers' own trades within 90 days instead of only annual disclosures.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to prohibit buying or selling securities or commodities while in possession of material nonpublic information about pending legislation obtained through Congress or federal employment [S2][S3].

Adds a rule to the House Code of Official Conduct barring House members, officers, and employees from disclosing nonpublic legislative information when they have reason to believe it will be used to trade [S3].

Requires members of Congress and covered legislative-branch employees to report any stock, bond, or commodities-futures transaction of $1,000 or more to the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate within 90 days, rather than waiting for an annual filing [S3].

Brings political-intelligence consultants and firms—businesses paid to gather information from officials for market analysis—under the same registration and disclosure requirements that apply to lobbyists [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, congressional staff, other federal employees, and political-intelligence firms, who would lose an information advantage in the markets and face new reporting and registration paperwork.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the definition of 'material nonpublic information' about legislation to SEC rulemaking, and legislative information is far fuzzier than corporate inside information, so enforcement could be difficult and genuinely routine government contacts could be caught up in it [S3].
The 90-day transaction report still lets a lawmaker trade up to three months before the public learns of it [S3].
The disclosure-and-leaking rule added to House ethics rules covers only House personnel, not senators or executive-branch officials, leaving a gap the securities rules only partially fill [S3].

Extending lobbyist-style registration to political-intelligence contacts could sweep in legitimate conversations with officials, which is why the bill had to write in an exception for journalists gathering news [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it targets conduct ordinary investors cannot match, trading on what the government is about to do before the public knows. The costs are mainly compliance burdens and the difficulty of writing a workable definition, since information about legislation spreads through countless ordinary conversations. The bill's own media and definitional carve-outs show drafters recognized this, but the reporting window and the House-only ethics rule left the design partly unfinished. On balance the trade restriction and disclosure requirements outweigh the administrative cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees when introduced, was sent to two subcommittees, and sat there for the rest of the Congress with no further action before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Baird of Washington, joined by Rep. Louise Slaughter of New York, introduced the bill on May 16, 2007 [S3].
The Speaker referred it to the Financial Services Committee and additionally to the committees on House Administration, Judiciary, Agriculture, and Standards of Official Conduct [S3][S5].
In late June 2007 it was referred to subcommittees on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties (Judiciary) and on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management (Agriculture) [S5].
No markup, vote, or report followed; the action history ends with the subcommittee referrals, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their staff, along with political-intelligence firms, kept the ability to trade on and sell nonpublic legislative information with no new disclosure requirements, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and political-intelligence firms

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan (9 of the 10 cosponsors were Democrats, 1 a Republican), but because no committee or floor vote ever occurred, the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.note: These firms make money gathering nonpublic information from officials and selling it to market traders, an advantage ordinary investors do not have. The bill would have forced them to register and disclose their contacts with officials just as lobbyists must.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and congressional staff
industries.note: Lawmakers and employees would have been barred from trading on information only they hold and would have had to report their own trades within 90 days. The bill died without a vote, leaving that position intact.
Funds that buy legislative intelligence to trade ahead of the public would have lost a source of legal advantage under the new trading prohibitions.
